cells.tense: The scales are in your hand right now, and your hand is steady.
cells.ask: offer the level ground you can already see to something that's ending, and let it close clean
cells.core:
You feel the proportions without working them out. What's owed and what's given pass between people and you keep them level the way you keep your balance walking — no tally, no strain, just the evenness holding. That steadiness works on in the background, mostly unnamed.

What it has room to feed next is an ending. Something in your life has finished and is waiting for you to say so — and the same sureness that keeps your exchanges square can be turned to that, making room for what hasn't arrived yet. The scales don't need protecting. They need to be used.
cells.sheetLine: You keep things level without keeping score, and you can spend that steadiness on an ending that's due.
cells.verb: squaring what's out of true until the two sides meet level
cells.place: the clear room where shape shows through the thing that carries it

cells.tense: You're already living past the moment you're in, running the ledger forward before anything's actually owed.
cells.ask: hold one thing without settling it — let it stay unresolved a while and carry that
cells.core:
The sense of what's fair has turned into a running account. Every kindness gets a column, every slight gets a line, and you know the total before the day ends. What used to flow now gets tracked — and the tracking has become the relationship, though nobody watching would call it that.

When this is working it's simpler: you notice the imbalance, you correct it, you move on. Holding without forcing is what's called for here — the strength to carry a real wrong or a real debt without needing it resolved on your schedule. Not everything outstanding has to be closed today.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping books on things meant to flow, and the tally costs more than the debt.

cells.tense: There's a doorway you're standing in front of that your body already walked past.
cells.ask: practice, once a day, saying what's actually owed to you without dressing it up or softening it
cells.core:
You can see what's fair as clearly as anyone — the pattern is right there — and you don't reach for your share of it. Things get taken from you and you let them go, and the evenness you know is right stays theoretical, never claimed. The seeing isn't the problem. The asking is.

What rebuilds it isn't force, it's repetition. A small practice, done quietly and often, until saying the true thing gets easier than swallowing it — like any skill, it comes back through the hands, not the will. The point isn't to make you harder. It's to let the fairness you can already see reach the table.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's fair and you don't claim it, and practice brings it back, not proof.

cells.tense: You're adding up a column of numbers you didn't notice you were writing down.
cells.ask: ask yourself plainly what you already know about a thing you keep scoring, and let the answer stand
cells.core:
Somewhere under the day you're keeping count — who's owed what, who got more, who hasn't paid — and if asked you'd say you weren't thinking about it at all. The weighing runs on its own. You didn't authorize it and you don't feel responsible for it, which is exactly why it keeps going.

When it's yours, it's lighter: you sense what's out of proportion and act, without needing to explain why it's obvious. That kind of knowing doesn't argue — it just lands, and you can trust it because it's already yours. The tally isn't foreign to you. It just hasn't been picked up and read.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping a count you didn't know about, and you already know what's on it.
